en: Instruction on the Vyāla: Now I shall proclaim the instruction that follows the system of the Vyāla-muni, which is joined with the euphonic combinations of words (*padasandhi*) as well as the euphonic combinations of vowels (*svarasandhi*). 1.
The sixfold repetition of a word is called *jaṭā*.
One should repeat twice the collection of words as they appear in the sequential order;
then, having repeated the preceding [word] twice, one should conclude it with the second [word].
In this same manner, one should conclude with the second half-verse by reciting it over the subsequent [word];
thus, having recited the middle word once, the *jaṭā* consists of three words, which is the sequential order.
Having repeated the final [hemistich] twice, one should recite the middle one once.
Then, having repeated the preceding one twice, one should recite the middle one once;
thus, at the conclusion, the wrapping of the half-verses shall occur as in the *krama* method.
Thus is the *jaṭā* of the three-fold sequence;
one should practice the garland as if it were a *jaṭā*. The first and penultimate words are prescribed, and the sequence and its reverse order were previously proclaimed by the great sage Vyāla.

Having thus explained the sequence of the garland (mālākrama), and having reversed it once more, one should conclude the end [of the practice] upon the crest-lock (śikhā) or the matted hair (jaṭā). 7.
Thus, one should practice the *śikhā* like matted locks (*jaṭā*); having joined the latter half-verse with the former,
one should conclude with two [half-verses] as a single matted lock, just as it was previously explained by the great seer Vyāsa.
Thus, the lines are said to be two, three, or four in sequence; or else, the group [of syllables] is stated in sequence within the *ṛc*.
In this manner the staff (*daṇḍa*) is described; one should conclude it at the end of the half-verse. 9.

Having thus stated the *daṇḍa* and the *krama*, and having again reversed the order, one should speak the subsequent *krama* by skipping over that; then, like a chariot, one should proceed up to the end of the *ṛc* according to the *krama*. 10.

Thus, having repeated the *ratha* twice over the *jaṭottara*, and each one of the *madhyama* and so forth both as a junction (*sandhi*) and in sequence, it is called *ghana* by the wise. Thus ends the *ghana*.
One should practice the sequence of these three starting from the crest;
or else, having wound the end around the matted locks, it is called "dense" by the serpent [i.e., the commentator].
(12) This is an alternative reading.
Thus ends the Vyālaśikṣā.
